title: What is MCP and Why It's a Big Deal

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll be able to explain what MCP is, why the open standard matters, how the architecture works at a high level, and what kinds of tools it unlocks — in plain English, to anyone. You'll also understand the 2026 ecosystem and which MCP servers are most widely used.

No code yet. Just the mental model.

## Before MCP: Claude in a Box

Before MCP, Claude only knew what was inside the conversation window. You had to paste in every piece of context manually — file contents, search results, calendar data, database records.

Claude was powerful, but isolated. Like a brilliant consultant locked in a room with no phone, no laptop, and no window to the outside world.

With MCP, that changes completely. Claude can now:
- Read and write files on your computer
- Query your email inbox
- Search GitHub repositories
- Run queries against a database
- Control a real web browser
- Check your calendar
- Search documentation for any library

The information flows to Claude automatically, on demand, without you copying and pasting anything.
**The one-sentence version:** MCP is the standard plug that lets Claude connect to any external tool — the same way USB lets a computer connect to any device.

## The USB Analogy

Before USB existed, every peripheral — mouse, keyboard, printer, camera — needed its own special port. Hardware manufacturers had to build a different connector for every device and every computer.

USB changed that. One standard port. Any device. Plug in, it works.

MCP does the same thing for AI and tools.

**Before MCP:**
- Every tool needed its own custom integration with every AI model
- OpenAI built its own plugins system, Google built its own, Anthropic built its own
- Developers had to write different code for every combination of AI + tool
- An integration built for ChatGPT didn't work with Claude

**With MCP:**
- One standard protocol that any AI client and any tool can implement
- Build one MCP server for your database → it works with Claude, Cursor, Zed, and any other MCP-compatible client
- Build one MCP client (like Claude Code) → it connects to any MCP server anyone builds
- Integrations are reusable across the entire ecosystem

This is why it's a big deal. It's not a feature — it's a standard.

## How MCP Architecture Works

MCP uses a client-server architecture. Understanding this helps you debug issues and understand what's possible:

**MCP Hosts (clients):** Applications that want AI + tool integration. Examples: Claude Code, Claude.ai Desktop App, Cursor, Zed, VS Code extensions. Each host can connect to multiple MCP servers simultaneously.

**MCP Servers:** Programs that expose tools, resources, or prompts to any compatible host. Examples: a GitHub server that exposes issue/PR operations, a filesystem server that exposes file read/write, a PostgreSQL server that exposes database queries.

**How they communicate:** MCP servers communicate with hosts over one of two transports:
- **stdio** (Standard Input/Output): The host launches the server as a child process and communicates over stdin/stdout. Used for local servers.
- **HTTP/SSE** (Server-Sent Events): The server runs as a web service. Used for remote servers or servers shared across multiple users.

**The request flow:**
1. You type: `"List my open GitHub issues"`
2. Claude Code identifies this needs the GitHub tool `list_issues`
3. Claude Code sends the tool call to the GitHub MCP server
4. The GitHub MCP server calls the GitHub API and gets the response
5. The response comes back to Claude Code and Claude incorporates it into its answer

From your perspective: you asked a question in plain English and got an answer. Behind the scenes: two programs (Claude Code and the GitHub server) communicated via the MCP protocol.

**Security model:** MCP servers run on your machine (for local servers) or on trusted infrastructure (for remote). They use your existing credentials — your GitHub token, your Google OAuth session, your database connection string. Claude never sees your credentials directly; the MCP server does, and returns data to Claude.

## Why the Open Standard Matters

MCP is open. Anyone can read the specification at modelcontextprotocol.io. Anyone can build an MCP server. Anyone can build an MCP client.

This means:
- A developer can build an MCP server for their company's internal tool, and it just works with Claude Code
- A startup can ship an MCP server alongside their product and get AI integration for free
- A hobbyist can build an MCP server for their home automation system
- A tool you use at work can add MCP support and become instantly usable by Claude

The open standard creates a compounding ecosystem effect. As of mid-2026, hundreds of MCP servers already exist:

| Category | Popular servers |
|----------|----------------|
| **Development** | GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear, Sentry |
| **Productivity** | Gmail, Google Calendar, Slack, Notion, Todoist |
| **Databases** | PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, Redis, MongoDB |
| **Files & Storage** | Filesystem, Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive |
| **Browser** | Playwright, Puppeteer (web scraping + automation) |
| **Documentation** | Context7 (library docs), AWS docs, Azure docs |
| **Communication** | Discord, Microsoft Teams, Twilio |
| **APIs** | Stripe, Shopify, Salesforce, HubSpot |

And the list grows every week. Because the protocol is open, the ecosystem compounds — each new server adds value for all MCP clients.

**MCP was created by Anthropic** and released as an open standard in November 2024. It has since been adopted by Cursor, Zed, VS Code extensions, JetBrains, Windsurf, and other AI coding tools. The official specification lives at modelcontextprotocol.io. The GitHub repository at github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers contains official reference servers maintained by Anthropic.

## The Three Things MCP Servers Can Expose

Every MCP server exposes one or more of three things:

**1. Tools — Actions Claude can take:**
The most common type. Each tool has a name, description, and input schema.
Examples: `send_email`, `create_github_issue`, `run_sql_query`, `click_button_in_browser`.
Tools have inputs (what you pass in) and outputs (what they return).

Claude decides when to call a tool based on your request. If you ask "create a GitHub issue for this bug," Claude recognises it needs the `create_issue` tool and calls it automatically.

**2. Resources — Data Claude can read:**
Read-only windows into external data. Think of them like files or API endpoints.
Examples: `file://path/to/file`, `github://repo/issues`, `postgres://table/users`.
Resources are used when Claude needs context rather than to take an action.

**3. Prompts — Pre-written prompt templates:**
Less commonly used. Let MCP servers package useful interaction patterns that users can invoke. More relevant to building custom products than to day-to-day use.

**In practice:** 90% of what you'll do with MCP in this course is tool use. When you ask Claude to "list my emails" or "search my codebase," it's calling tools that MCP servers expose.

## What This Part of the Course Covers

Part 8 is a hands-on tour through the most useful MCP servers available today:

- **8-2:** Installing your first MCP server — the filesystem server
- **8-3:** MCP configuration — `settings.json` structure for MCP servers
- **8-4:** GitHub MCP — issues, PRs, code search
- **8-5:** Gmail + Google Calendar
- **8-6:** Playwright browser automation
- **8-7:** Database MCP (SQLite)
- **8-8:** Notion and productivity tools
- **8-9:** Context7 — live documentation for any library
- **8-10:** Slack and team communication
- **8-11:** Building your own MCP server from scratch

By the end of Part 8, Claude will have access to your files, your GitHub, your email, your calendar, your browser, and a database — and you'll know how to add any other tool that has an MCP server.

**Security first with MCP:** Each MCP server has access to something valuable — your email, your GitHub, your database. Before installing any MCP server:
1. Only install from trusted sources (official Anthropic servers, well-known open source projects)
2. Review what permissions the server requests
3. Never connect MCP servers to production databases or sensitive data stores during learning
4. Remember: Claude can use MCP tools autonomously — if you give it access to email, it can send email. Permission prompts protect you; don't disable them.

sections.title: Your MCP Wishlist
sections.content:
Before we install anything, spend 5 minutes thinking about what you'd actually want Claude to have access to. This shapes which MCP servers you prioritise.

Open `notes/mcp-wishlist.md` in VS Code (create it if needed) and answer:

**1. Which 3 tools do you use every single day** where AI assistance would save you the most time?

Examples to spark thinking:
- Email: drafting replies, summarising threads, finding information buried in conversations
- Calendar: scheduling, finding free time, understanding your week at a glance
- GitHub/GitLab: understanding what's changed, what's open, what needs attention
- Your company's project tracker (Jira, Linear, Notion)
- A database you regularly query
- A codebase you need to understand

**2. What's the most repetitive task you do** that follows a clear pattern — the kind of thing where you think 'this could probably be automated'?

**3. What data does Claude currently lack access to** that would make its answers dramatically more accurate or relevant?

Examples: your actual email history, your team's actual codebase, your real project status, your company's actual documentation.

**4. From the MCP server table above**, which 3 servers would you prioritise installing first?

Write your answers in `notes/mcp-wishlist.md` and save it. These answers will guide your priorities through the lessons ahead — the servers that matter to your actual work are worth doing thoroughly. The others you can skim.

**Format:**
```markdown
# My MCP Priorities

## Top 3 tools I use daily
1. 
2. 
3. 

## Most repetitive task

## Data Claude lacks that would help most

## Top 3 MCP servers to install
1. 
2. 
3. 
```

sections.question: A team is building an internal tool that queries their company database and presents results in a chat interface. They want it to work with Claude, Cursor, and any future AI tools their team adopts. What architecture choice gives them the most flexibility?
options: Build a direct API integration with each AI tool separately — customised for each one's specific format
Build an MCP server that exposes the database queries as tools — any MCP-compatible AI client can then use it without changes
Build a webhook integration with each AI tool — webhooks are more widely supported than MCP
Use a proprietary integration platform (like Zapier) rather than building their own server
sections.explanation: Building an MCP server is the right answer for future-proofing. Because MCP is an open standard adopted by Claude Code, Cursor, Zed, VS Code extensions, and more, you build once and it works with every compliant client. Building separate integrations for each AI tool (option A) means n-times the work and ongoing maintenance as new tools emerge. The key insight from the USB analogy: the value of a standard multiplies as adoption grows. An MCP server built today works with every MCP client released in the future.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 8-1.** You understand what MCP is (open standard for AI-tool integration), why it matters (ecosystem compounds with adoption), how the architecture works (client-server with stdio or HTTP), and what the three server primitives are (tools, resources, prompts). Next: installing your first MCP server.
